reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The most common recognised cause is gestational alloimmune liver disease (GALD), an alloimmune process rather than a primary genetic iron-handling defect
It presents as severe neonatal liver failure with coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, jaundice, hypoglycaemia, and often intrauterine growth restriction
There is extrahepatic siderosis, with iron deposition in sites such as the pancreas, heart, and salivary glands, while sparing the reticuloendothelial system
Markedly raised ferritin with high transferrin saturation is characteristic but not specific
Diagnosis is supported by demonstrating extrahepatic iron, classically by lip (minor salivary gland) biopsy or magnetic resonance imaging
The condition has a very high recurrence rate in subsequent pregnancies of the same mother, which has important management implications
Treatment centres on exchange transfusion and intravenous immunoglobulin to remove and neutralise the offending alloantibody, with liver transplantation reserved for refractory failure
reference.pathophysiology: In gestational alloimmune liver disease, maternal immunoglobulin G antibodies directed against a fetal hepatocyte antigen cross the placenta and activate the complement cascade on fetal liver cells, causing widespread hepatocyte injury and necrosis in utero. The resulting fetal liver failure disturbs the regulation of iron transport across the placenta, leading to excessive iron loading of fetal tissues. Iron therefore accumulates in the liver and in extrahepatic parenchymal sites such as the pancreas, heart, and salivary and other glands, characteristically sparing the reticuloendothelial system. The severe hepatic dysfunction present at birth reflects damage that began during gestation, and the same maternal alloimmunity tends to recur in later pregnancies.
additionalDifferentials: Perinatal viral hepatitis and congenital infections
Inherited metabolic disease such as tyrosinaemia and mitochondrial disorders
Other causes of neonatal acute liver failure
additionalInvestigations: Coagulation studies and markers of synthetic liver function
Lip (minor salivary gland) biopsy to demonstrate extrahepatic siderosis
Magnetic resonance imaging to detect extrahepatic iron deposition
Metabolic and infective screen to exclude other causes of neonatal liver failure
Placental and, where relevant, postmortem examination to support the diagnosis
redFlags: Severe coagulopathy unresponsive to vitamin K signalling advanced liver failure
Rapid clinical deterioration despite supportive care
A history of prior affected pregnancy or unexplained fetal loss indicating high recurrence risk
reference.prognosis: Untreated the condition carries a very high mortality from neonatal liver failure, but alloimmune-directed therapy and, when needed, liver transplantation have improved survival; recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common and can be mitigated by maternal treatment during gestation.
pitfalls: Assuming it is a primary genetic iron-overload disorder rather than an alloimmune process
Relying on raised ferritin alone, which is neither sensitive nor specific
Failing to demonstrate extrahepatic siderosis to support the diagnosis
Overlooking the high recurrence risk and the opportunity for maternal treatment in future pregnancies
Delaying alloimmune-directed therapy while awaiting confirmatory tests in a deteriorating neonate
